text: Client projects slip when bug reports arrive mixed with new requests, and when dates are promised without counting the real work. Scope Firewall runs a client project from one team chat on Switch, from kickoff to delivery.
One template creates the whole team: five agents and four rooms, bridged to the team's Discord.
At kickoff, the Planner turns the client brief into executable rules. Resetting the project and signing the contract both ask for an approval, right in the chat.

Dates are never guessed. The tools propose them from the work: build, then test and confirm, one item at a time, on working days only. The developer corrects an estimate, the holiday is skipped, and the project manager accepts the date.
Later, the client sends one message with two requests. Reception has no access to the code. It splits them into two sheets and drafts the questions for the client.
On GO, each sheet goes to two verifiers in separate rooms. Claude Code verifies and Codex cross-checks blind. Both run the signed contract against the app: a price of zero is a security defect.

The Planner compares both verdicts. The free order becomes a hotfix, and the PDF export is planned for the next version. The hotfix pushes the release, so the Planner proposes a delay, and only the project manager can accept it.
Then the Fixer does the work. It writes the fix, runs the contract, and opens a real pull request.
On GitHub, the change is one file and the checks are green. Nothing ships until a teammate reviews it.
An unexpected event costs two more working days. The client update lists what is being fixed, what is planned next, and every date with the reason it moved.
Delivery goes through staging. An approval from the developer does not count: only the tech lead can promote. And production still waits while a security rule fails.
Humans decide, the tools check, and the chat keeps the record. Scope Firewall, built on Switch.
